#65438. An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting.
  • Recent findings suggest that that is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating.
  • The fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “major three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting. Each leader has pronounced himself satisfied with their discussion. But if their concluding statement is an accurate reflection of what was remarked in the closed session, little of any real consequence — with one possible exception — was agreed to, which was only to be expected. Much has been made by some of the symbolism of the meeting. Did it signal that a disreputable carve-up, even a latest Yalta, was underway? If that was the plan, the result, appropriately and mercifully, looks like a package with more than a touch of Temu about it.

Recent findings suggest that that is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating. Trump’s earlier, overly enthusiastic greeting of his “friend” Putin — the aggressor, after all, in a genocidal war — was not only nauseating but also careless. It sent a disturbing signal to the rest of NATO, an organization that still plays a critical role in maintaining American security as well as peace, however uneasy, in Europe west of Ukraine. It is to be hoped that Trump’s delight at the sight of his supposed pal was, to use a word often applied to this president’s approach to diplomacy, transactional, a display of a dealmaker’s schmooze and nothing more.

The fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “major three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away. Russia is economically enfeebled and embroiled in a brutally and humiliatingly debilitating war, but it remains a vast, resource-rich country that, militarily anyway, counts as a superpower and one that, as Ukrainians can testify, is still capable of wreaking immense destruction. The more interesting symbolism was detectable in the various gestures through which Xi Jinping emphasized during Putin’s visit that Russia is China’s junior partner. That, too, is today’s reality.

Industry observers note that as alluded to above, the joint statement issued after the meeting was, as should have been expected, thin gruel. There was talk of reforming the U.N. “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its fundamental mission of maintaining international peace and security.” If that implies reining in Turtle Bay’s efforts to extend supranational (and thus post-democratic) governance, that’s no bad thing, but in practice little will probably change.

Recent findings suggest that in a similar vein, the trio, whose countries have not submitted to the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, implicitly criticized the attempted extension of its reach. They stressed the need for “respect for immunities of State officials,” a subject doubtless close to Putin’s heart. There is no need to grumble too much about this. The ICC is highly politicized, and, while it does not constitute much of a deterrent, it may even provide a perverse incentive to wrongdoers to hang onto power. Putin deserves to face judgment, but a better place for that would be Kyiv, not The Hague.

And all three declared that they planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” If that reflected some post-midterms unease on Trump’s part, that, as an admission of weakness, would have been a message better not sent. It would also be a mistake, despite recent waivers, for the U.S. to abandon its general application of sanctions on Iranian and Russian oil (the Europeans, incidentally, could do a better job of enforcing theirs). No pressure should be put on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure other than as part of a general “energy cease-fire” such as that floated earlier this year, which Ukraine was willing to accept.

Sources indicate that no details have been released so far of what was said in the meeting about Ukraine. However, Putin has been reiterating his hard line, supplemented by an absurd and aggressive proposal to rewrite Europe’s security architecture. Hopefully, Trump was not misled by any bonhomie in Shenzhen, although some accounts of his later call with European leaders were not entirely encouraging in that respect.

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump participate in a trilateral meeting during the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.

To return to reality: China has no interest in helping end the war in Ukraine, and Russia’s ambitions in Europe are such that the eventual consequences of undermining Kyiv’s ability to resist won’t stop at Ukraine’s borders. Speaking of which, we hope that Trump warned Xi and Putin that the growing intensity of “gray zone” activity, from drones in Leipzig Airport to cyberattacks on both sides of the Atlantic, risks triggering retaliation that could easily spiral into something extremely dangerous.

Any claims that the Shenzhen meeting has delivered the death blow to the post-1945 order would be overblown, akin to complaining about the murder of a corpse. The postwar settlement has been in flux for decades — Nixon, after all, went to China — a process that has accelerated, along with dramatic shifts in relative global economic and political power, since the Soviet collapse. But although the landscape has changed, Trump should pay more attention to America’s successful management of the (first) Cold War. Alliances matter, deterrence works, strength is rewarded, and aggression by, or sponsored by, hostile powers and their proxies should be contained and, where possible, reversed.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

On “An Overhyped Trilateral Summit”.

Mexico’s President Spent 21 Hours In Coach Getting To China—And Sat In A Middle Seat

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines.
  • According to recent reports, that’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar.
  • The 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines. She reportedly sat in 33B. A middle seat, on a trip across the Pacific, to represent her country at a summit of world leaders. That’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar. But while Sheinbaum is winning praise for saving taxpayers money, she should have flown business class. The 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Here’s her departure patch: Claudia Sheinbaum’s update on her trip to Shenzhen, November 15, 2026 21 Hours Includes The Stop In Tijuana She left Mexico City early Sunday, November 15, on China Southern flight CZ8032 and arrived in Shenzhen on Monday. The Airbus A350-900 made its scheduled technical stop in Tijuana along the way. The first flight took 3 hours 12 minutes and the transpacific segment clocked in at 14 hours 56 minutes, with about two and a half hours on the ground between them. China Southern operates the route nonstop from Shenzhen to Mexico City, with the Tijuana stop in the other direction. Several stories report that seat 33B is in the back of the aircraft. In fact, it’s the front of standard economy. On arrival she posted video of her welcome in Shenzhen. An airport bus brought her to the red carpet, where an honor guard and performers waited. She received a presidential welcome. Which reminds me a little bit of when I’ve booked first class awards on Lufthansa, but the intra-European segment was only available in coach. Nobody ever could quite figure out how a coach passenger had a vehicle waiting for them on the tarmac. She returned on China Southern flight CZ8031 and shared a photo with the crew: Claudia Sheinbaum thanks the crew of flight CZ8031 on her return from Shenzhen Mexico Sold Its Presidential 787 Sheinbaum is continuing a practice established by Andrés Manuel López Obrador. In July 2020, I wrote about Mexico’s president flying Delta coach and connecting in Atlanta to meet Trump. He had an exit row aisle seat on a Delta flight from Mexico City. Delta was blocking middle seats at the time, too, due to the pandemic. Reforma’s video of López Obrador boarding Delta for his Washington trip, July 7, 2020 López Obrador refused to use Mexico’s presidential Boeing 787-8. After years of trying to find a buyer, Mexico sold it to Tajikistan for about $92 million in 2023. He remarked the proceeds would fund two hospitals. This isn’t Sheinbaum’s first long trip in coach, either. In April I covered her economy trip to Europe, flying through Madrid to Barcelona and returning to Mexico City on Aeromexico. She posted a photo of herself working at her coach seat: Claudia Sheinbaum working during her April 2026 trip to Barcelona I thought that was performative then. A president’s time has value, and so does being rested for the work the country is sending her to do. Aeromexico business class would have provided better rest and opportunity to work. Pringles, Princes, And A Qatari 747 I’ve covered plenty of politicians and royals flying coach. Prince William flew American Airlines economy from Memphis to Dallas in 2014, in a bulkhead window seat on an Airbus A319. He’s also flown Ryanair and taken the family on Flybe, carrying their hand luggage. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle flew British Airways coach to Nice for Fresh Year’s in 2017. They and three bodyguards occupied the last three rows, with empty seats around them. T Argentina’s Javier Milei flew coach on his trip to Davos in January 2024. Given Argentina’s finances and the spending cuts he wanted the public to accept, there was a political purpose for the symbolism. David Cameron was photographed eating Pringles and working on his iPad aboard easyJet in 2015, while traveling to Portugal. I liked that one. William and Harry’s grandfather Prince Philip, though, described the improvements in air travel over his lifetime with the qualification, “provided you don’t travel in something called economy class, which sounds ghastly.” Meanwhile, thhe Pentagon accepted Qatar’s Boeing 747-8 in May 2025 for Trump’s use as Air Force One. It was widely described as a $400 million gift. I covered the Qatari jet’s conversion this summer, including the decision to preserve its luxury interior and the initiative for it eventually to go to Trump’s presidential library. The U.S. president needs secure communications, protection, and the ability to keep working while traveling. That can justify dedicated aircraft. Sheinbaum’s coach trip earned publicity, including favorable attention in China while she was there to meet its leaders. But saving the difference between coach and business class is simply a poor value tradeoff when the cost is productive time and sleep for someone with a high opportunity cost. #65436. House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
  • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
  • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

“My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., stated earlier this year.

The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

According to recent reports, “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., mentioned during the meeting.

When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

“I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

It comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

“The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she said in a statement earlier this week.

Cammack mentioned that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

“Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack mentioned in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., said everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

“We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he noted at Thursday’s meeting.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, mentioned additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress.
  • The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, mentioned additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

According to recent reports, senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

Recent findings suggest that as they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

In a recent development, “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

It has been revealed that as of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

As with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

According to recent reports, last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

In a recent development, on Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

In a recent development, “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, said at a news conference.

It has been revealed that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office mentioned in a news release.

Sources indicate that “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet mentioned in a statement.

Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

“Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., stated Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

As with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

Recent findings suggest that the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

Industry observers note that john M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”.

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”.

Industry observers note that “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump stated midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”.

Sources indicate that the last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the Newly introduced York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

In a recent development, meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. #65427. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

📅 16 Jul 2018 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1866 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

📅 16 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses.
  • Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.
  • Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s latest endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney notes in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

Recent findings suggest that you can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Recent findings suggest that nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare initiative. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne indicates.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show.

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

It has been revealed that but this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

Sources indicate that (To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” remarked to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most key topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.).

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he states are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Industry observers note that baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

Recent findings suggest that but her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

According to recent reports, (Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.).

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

According to recent reports, this has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”.

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran indicates, arming teachers is crazy.

Industry observers note that and this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

In a recent development, yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two latest characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

Industry observers note that to other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#65426. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

📅 23 Oct 2020 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1955 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

“Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

📅 23 Oct 2020 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.
  • Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one.
  • All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Sources indicate that performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

Industry observers note that and this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

According to recent reports, tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

In a recent development, when Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a upcoming mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”.

Industry observers note that this is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

Recent findings suggest that in the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

It has been revealed that now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

It has been revealed that the sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”.

Sources indicate that following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half. Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

It has been revealed that there’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen confirmed that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”.

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Recent findings suggest that nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Recent findings suggest that fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

It has been revealed that then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”.

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?).

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

Recent findings suggest that there’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” indicates without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”.

All of these are women, by the way.

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

It has been revealed that at the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

“Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is presently streaming on Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photo Credit: The Riyadh Skyline Wikimedia Commons / B.alotaby.

In a recent development, riyadh’s hotels lost their peak season when the airport shut. With BA, Cathay Pacific and others suspended into the new year and Houthi strikes still hitting the capital, the recovery hasn’t started.

Riyadh hotels had one of their worst months of the year in October. A temporary shutdown of the city’s main airport cut off inbound demand just as peak season started.

In a recent development, occupancy fell 34.7 percentage points year over year to 34.3% from 69%, according to CoStar’s STR. Only March had lower occupancy, at 28.3%. Average daily rate dropped 29.9% to $190 and revenue per available room (RevPAR) fell 65.1% to $65.

“October and November are usually the peak season months for Riyadh, so the impact is much bigger,” said Kostas Nikolaidis, associate account director for Middle East and Africa at STR.

The October demand collapse traces back to an attack on King Khalid International Airport. The airport closed after an attack on Oct. 10 that Saudi authorities mentioned killed 13 people and injured more than 300. Some 86% of scheduled Riyadh departures were canceled between Oct. 8 and late October, according to Cirium data, Skift repor.

#65421. Tech Report: “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2342 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.
  • In a recent development, since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting.
  • The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article originally appeared on ProPublica.

As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

In a recent development, since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.

The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

Recent findings suggest that courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.

“The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” noted Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”.

In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson remarked Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”.

The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”.

Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

Recent findings suggest that republicans will focus on problems such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, stated.

Here are five concerns that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:.

An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

According to recent reports, mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.

“Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they highlighted up in their official vehicles,” Earley noted.

It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

According to recent reports, nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.

Industry observers note that “We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown mentioned. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”.

A DOJ spokesperson noted “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”.

In a recent development, it’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers stated they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.

Federal officials have made clear they proposal to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.

On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”.

This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.

It has been revealed that in a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis highlighted. Some said on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.

Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”.

In a recent development, A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation strategy” that would interfere with legal voting.

In a recent development, last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”.

In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”.

Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She said the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”.

Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”.

Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.

A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

“A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” stated David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.

States often change laws and rules related to voting.

Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.

Sources indicate that A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under upcoming rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.

Industry observers note that texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.

In a recent development, voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two complications involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand fresh voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.

Every election features some problems with voting equipment.

So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.

Sources indicate that ES&S, the organization that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they noted.

Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes mentioned “the fear it caused was real.”.

In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, stated the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.

“States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he remarked.

Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.

Recent findings suggest that late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.

Trump has mentioned he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The Newly introduced York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.

Nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

“This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the Washington attorney general.

In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which noted the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.).

Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block newly introduced members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

“I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.

In a recent development, that’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

In a recent development, in the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.

To many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

Sources indicate that these policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

Black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.

Almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.

In a recent development, this year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

It has been revealed that they may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

Industry observers note that after 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.

In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a massive Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.

According to recent reports, louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

We need your help to stay independent.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent New York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the substantial tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.

Sources indicate that they have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.
