📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s speech last week excoriating the rule of law, and taking particular aim at the International Criminal Court, is a sharp reminder that the United States under the Trump administration has become a rogue state.

In a recent development, it was especially jarring to see America’s top diplomat attack the notion of international law just ahead of a three-power summit in China that will see the United States matched against—or in concert with—China and Russia. For decades, the United States has championed international law and respect for global norms as a way to contrast its behavior with rivals that carry out genocides and war crimes. That contrast is every day dimmer, by design.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s speech last week excoriating the rule of law, and taking particular aim at the International Criminal Court, is a sharp reminder that the United States under the Trump administration has become a rogue state.

Industry observers note that it was especially jarring to see America’s top diplomat attack the notion of international law just ahead of a three-power summit in China that will see the United States matched against—or in concert with—China and Russia. For decades, the United States has championed international law and respect for global norms as a way to contrast its behavior with rivals that carry out genocides and war crimes. That contrast is every day dimmer, by design.

According to recent reports, “At the State Department, we have seen the same thing firsthand in the realm of what is called international law. We’ve heard the concept international law invoked against nearly every major foreign-policy decision or action of this administration,” Rubio mentioned in a speech to the Federalist Society, a group of conservative lawyers. “For this global elite, international law is not a neutral body of rules; international law is an instrument, an instrument to advance their interests under the pretense of universal principles.”.

Sources indicate that rubio focused much of his ire on the International Criminal Court (ICC), a body created more than two decades ago to prosecute the very worst transnational crimes, including genocide and crimes against humanity. Rubio called the ICC a “fake court which is an unelected world tribunal” and cheered U.S. President Donald Trump’s sanctions on members of the court. Those sanctions, which will be fully effective in the spring, are already creating havoc for judges and prosecutors on the court.

“If they’re foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general, Pompey, when he stated to those who were trying to invoke their cities’ charters against his legions. He said, ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords,’” Rubio said, a line later echoed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. (Neither man got the quote, from Plutarch, quite correct.).

The Trump administration’s cavalier approach to the rule of law is the end of an era.

Here’s what the rest of the world can do about it.

The landmark case will have wide-ranging impacts, including for the court’s forthcoming judgment on Israel.

Recent findings suggest that the jettisoning of even a modicum of respect for the rule of law was alarming to experts who have spent decades working to ensure that U.S. foreign policy upholds a rules-based system.

“I thought it was one of the most ignorant speeches given by a secretary of state I can ever recall,” said Harold Koh, who was the State Department’s legal advisor during the Obama administration and is now a professor at Yale Law School.

He noted that the opening lines of the U.S. Declaration of Independence justified the colonies’ rupture with England “out of a decent respect for the opinions of mankind.”.

“They have no appreciation for how international law has made our lives better. Nobody ever talked about air-traffic control until it broke, but international law is air-traffic control for the entire world,” Koh said.

The actions taken by the second Trump administration had already raised concern about a rash of lawlessness in the U.S. government, as Rubio acknowledged in his speech. From the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean, to the apparent targeting of civilian infrastructure in Iran, to the threats to annex Canada and Greenland, the Trump administration has long forsaken any pretense of legitimate behavior and support for international law, even when that would advance U.S. interests. Washington’s efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, for instance, and prevent Iran from regulating traffic in the waterway depend on adherence to international maritime law (as Rubio has previously noted).

Rubio’s attacks on the ICC, which codified between 1998 and 2002 the architecture of international justice that was created and carried out by the United States in the aftermath of World War II, is particularly striking. The court was created specifically to prosecute the very worst crimes, limited to genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and crimes of aggression.

Recent findings suggest that the ICC, long a target of suspicion for U.S. conservatives who fear that a supranational body will usurp U.S. sovereignty (even though the United States is not a party to the convention or the court), has issued controversial arrest warrants for many world leaders, including two who are favorites of the Trump administration.

The ICC issued a warrant for the arrest of Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2023 for the alleged mass kidnapping of Ukrainian children during the Russia-Ukraine war and for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2024 for alleged war crimes related to the war in Gaza.

Ambassadors of the more than 120 countries that are parties to the Rome Statute that created the ICC met at The Hague on Wednesday to discuss how to deal with threats from the United States, among other countries. There are also fears that Washington will sanction additional international bodies, including the International Court of Justice, which is slated to rule on alleged genocide committed by the junta in Myanmar. Legal experts say that such a ruling could lower the legal threshold for genocide, which could put countries including Israel in the crosshairs of future judicial actions.

Rubio’s speech, which follows similar bellicose messages and policies from other officials such as Hegseth and U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz, show the Trump administration’s disdain for the rules that underpinned the American century, Koh mentioned.

“International law sets default patterns of behavior. It’s like driving on the wrong side of the road—that leads to car crashes, and this leads to conflicts with allies,” Koh said.

Recent findings suggest that “How does attacking these institutions help us? Everybody knows the ICC is going to survive Marco Rubio,” he added.

Considering its long history, the hundreds of billions of dollars involved over decades, its growing controversy and symbol of the special bilateral relationship, U.S. aid to Israel came to an abrupt end this month with barely a whimper. Rather than being announced in a platitude-filled joint statement and with a roadmap for its gradual demise, the news that “by the end of this year, we won’t be paying Israel” emerged in an offhand remark by U.S. President Donald Trump seven minutes into an interview with Fox News on Nov. 3, the day of the midterm elections. It took three days for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly confirm the news, which he did by way of a on X. Israeli officials, who had been expecting the aid to unwind gradually after 2028 (when the current framework agreement expires) were taken by complete surprise.

Recent findings suggest that but none of that can conceal the fact that the aid program’s demise signals a major downgrade of U.S.-Israeli relations, one that is wholly an American initiative, not one of mutual consent as both Trump and Netanyahu presented it. Moreover, Israel is now losing a major component of U.S. ties at a moment when it is more politically and militarily dependent on the United States than at any time since the 1973 Yom Kippur War. And, even if Israel’s economy has become significant enough to cover the country’s military spending, its current capacity to do so is being tested by a major rearmament drive and the continued pursuit of an aggressive military policy that began after Hamas’s attack on Oct. 7, 2023.

According to recent reports, although it has had its ups and downs over the years, Israel long enjoined broad bipartisan support in Congress and in public opinion, certainly in comparison with the Palestinians, Israel’s main rival in the competition for American’s affections. That bipartisan consensus began to unravel 15 years ago under Netanyahu, who preferred the Republican Party and Christian evangelicals over Democrats and even the American Jewish community, whose liberal politics made it increasingly uncomfortable with Israeli policies.

Netanyahu’s alliance with the American right looked solid, but it crumbled in the wake of Hamas’s attack three years ago. The initial sympathy for Israel evaporated promptly as its offensive in Gaza proved unusually brutal and continued long after its military justification had run out. Not only did remaining support in the Democratic Party collapse, but Israel began losing the GOP, as well—starting at the far-right fringe of the MAGA movement and rapidly moving to the center, especially among younger Republicans. Israel’s role in convincing Trump to attack Iran earlier this year made it even more enemies across the political spectrum, as did the settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, which even succeeded in alienating many of Israel’s Christian supporters. A day after the midterm elections, U.S. Vice President JD Vance asserted that one of the four reasons Trump voters turned their backs on the GOP was that they wanted to “change our relationship to Israel.” Never one to mince words, Trump cited a “great dislike” for Israel as one reason for the Republicans’ defeat.

According to recent reports, in both parties, the $3.8 billion in annual U.S. aid had served as a flash point for anti-Israel sentiment. Progressives saw it as taxpayer dollars going to fund what they called “genocide” in Gaza; for MAGA Republicans, it violated the principals of “America first” and of U.S. allies standing on their own two feet. Netanyahu and his religious-right government shrugged off these dangerous developments. The far-right ideology that drives his government all but precluded policy changes that might have stemmed the growing hostility.

In purely money terms, the loss of U.S. aid isn’t critical for Israel. The annual amount that Israel gets hasn’t changed much over the years, but the Israeli economy has grown more than 20-fold. Thus, 40 years ago, aid was equal to about 11 percent of Israeli GDP; today, it is about 0.6 percent. Moreover, under the current 10-year framework, nearly all the aid money is today spent in the United States, so if anything, it harms the Israeli arms industry by reserving a major chunk of Israeli procurement contracts for U.S. makers. However, that isn’t the whole story. Aid accounted for about a fifth of the Israeli defense budget before Oct. 7. If it is 10 percent or less today, then that’s only because Israeli military spending has since tripled.

It is a testament to the strength of the Israeli economy and to the government’s strong finances (not to mention a vast increase in U.S. financial aid at the height of the Gaza war) that the country has been able to sustain such a vast increase, which, at close to 8 percent of GDP, is among the highest in the world. But the situation cannot continue indefinitely. The shock of the Hamas attack has left Israel feeling vulnerable, if for no other reason than that the conflicts with Iran, Hezbollah, and Hamas have not ended in a decisive victory. Netanyahu therefore wants to remain at elevated levels for the next decade. That involves not only more people in uniform than before Oct. 7, but a massive arms buildup that will saddle the economy with one of the world’s highest defense burdens for years to come. The loss of U.S. aid will mean that even more of the cost will fall on Israeli taxpayers than the government had planned on.

As it became evident over the past year that Trump wanted to gradually end the aid program (at the same time that European countries were increasingly refusing to sell Israel military gear and the risk was growing that U.S. arms purchases would be constrained by an increasingly critical Congress), Netanyahu began marketing the emerging threat as an opportunity for Israel to pursue a more independent military course.

Voters gave U.S. lawmakers a mandate to do more than just cut aid.

Democrats feel they have a mandate to put conditions on U.S. support for Israel.

That independence, however, will come at a cost, entailing the creation of an economy geared more heavily than ever to arms production. Turning Israel into what the prime minister has called a “super Sparta” will not only force the economy to produce the kind of arms and components that it could get more cheaply abroad, but it won’t seriously reduce Israeli dependence. Israel is a major producer of cutting-edge weaponry, but its industrial base is too small to make everything it needs, whether it’s a fighter jet or all of the thousands of tiny components that go into one.

According to recent reports, netanyahu’s Sparta is no substitute for Israel maintaining strong relations with the United States and its other partners. But, far from making Israel more independent, Netanyahu has done the reverse. U.S. financial aid and ammunition were critical for sustaining what turned out to be a lengthy war and occupation in the Gaza Strip, and the two assaults on Iran would not have been possible without direct U.S. military intervention. Netanyahu’s ambitions to remake the Middle East are too massive for Israel to undertake alone.

According to recent reports, in addition, the United States is Israel’s biggest trade partner, is by far its main source of foreign investment, and provides Israel with diplomatic cover in the United Nations. And, if that is not enough, Israel has no backup alliances to compensate for deteriorating ties with the United States. Quite to the contrary, the prime minister has presided over a severe deterioration in relations with Europe to the point that Israel is contending with increasingly severe sanctions.

According to recent reports, so, what lies ahead for bilateral ties? The end of aid marks a transition from relations predicated on broad domestic support in the United States for Israel—something akin to friendship—to a more transactional one based on mutual interests and the strategic value that each side brings to the table. That Israel will continue to need the United States in this newly introduced era is indisputable. The question is what Israel offers the United States, because it will now have to justify itself as an ally.

It is safe to say that intelligence-sharing and joint weapons development will remain valuable to Washington. But Israel’s previously crucial role as a force for regional stability has diminished. That is most evident in Syria, Lebanon, and Gaza, where, rather than helping Washington to bring at least a semblance of order and economic development, Israel has insisted on continuing to deploy troops in their respective territories and launch periodic attacks. It has rejected even tentative overtures by Syria and Lebanon to establish security arrangements and has blocked Trump’s effort to begin Gaza reconstruction. The White House has shown remarkable patience in the face of Israeli defiance, but that may no longer be the case now.

Industry observers note that and if the United States does finally disengage from the Middle East—an increasingly likely prospect in the wake of the Iran war debacle and the U.S. midterm elections—Israel may become just another second-tier power of little interest to Washington and with no influence there. That is a change that Israel can ill-afford to let happen.

Industry News: America and China Are Trying to Alter Their Economic Bargain

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The United States and China are locked in a derisking race.
  • Recent findings suggest that today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy.
  • The United States and China are locked in a derisking race.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The United States and China are locked in a derisking race. After decades of actively entwining their economies, both are now trying to achieve a degree of separation between them. Neither side seeks at this point to decouple completely from its rival. Each is trying instead to alter the terms of their economic relationship, reducing their own vulnerability to leverage, coercion or attacks that could damage its long-term prosperity and security, while working to acquire advantages over its counterparty. This is a struggle for power, waged through trade, investment and technology development.

Recent findings suggest that today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy. At the end of the Cold War, as after the two world wars, American policymakers were motivated by a mix of pragmatism and principle. They believed that there were enormous gains to be had from trade with large and potentially fast-growing markets. But they also hoped to bring to fruition the liberal dream of a ‘one-world’ global trading system in which freer flows of goods, capital and people would promote peace and freedom, as well as prosperity.

The United States and China are locked in a derisking race. After decades of actively entwining their economies, both are now trying to achieve a degree of separation between them. Neither side seeks at this point to decouple completely from its rival. Each is trying instead to alter the terms of their economic relationship, reducing their own vulnerability to leverage, coercion or attacks that could damage its long-term prosperity and security, while working to acquire advantages over its counterparty. This is a struggle for power, waged through trade, investment and technology development.

Today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy. At the end of the Cold War, as after the two world wars, American policymakers were motivated by a mix of pragmatism and principle. They believed that there were enormous gains to be had from trade with large and potentially fast-growing markets. But they also hoped to bring to fruition the liberal dream of a ‘one-world’ global trading system in which freer flows of goods, capital and people would promote peace and freedom, as well as prosperity.

In 1919 America had the world’s biggest economy, but the international political system was still multipolar, with other great powers in both Europe and Asia. Although Woodrow Wilson tried to persuade the victors, and his own people, of the wisdom of lowering tariff barriers and creating an open global trading system, both at home and abroad he lacked the ability to compel others to accept his ideas. Once rebuffed, America drew back into isolationism and protectionism. With no nation willing and able to hold it together, in the 1930s the global economy split apart.

By 1945 the world had become bipolar, with the United States and the Soviet Union standing above all other nations—and America alone briefly accounting for as much as half of global GDP. American planners at first entertained hopes of reviving Wilson’s vision, but the onset of the Cold War soon forced them to abandon the idea. Instead of cooperating to create a single unified system, each superpower proceeded to build its own largely separate bloc. Organised along predominantly liberal, free-market lines, the American-led bloc was ultimately able to out-produce, out-innovate, and out-last its Communist opponent.

With the demise of its former rival, the United States finally seemed set to restructure the entire world economy into a unified trading system. America and its allies hoped in the process to encourage the domestic transformation of their former enemies, preparing them to become members in good standing of what would finally be a globe-spanning liberal order.

The main instrument of this strategy in the economic realm was the World Trade Organization, and its most important target was China. To gain entry to the WTO China was required to make detailed commitments that, if followed, would bring its economic policies into closer alignment with liberal principles of open markets, limited state intervention and freer trade.

Recent findings suggest that political change was expected to follow close on the heels of economic liberalisation. Increased reliance on markets would lead to rising prosperity and, as had already happened in Western Europe and parts of Asia, the members of an expanding middle class would demand political rights to go with their growing economic freedoms.

American strategists knew that drawing China more fully into an expanding world economy would enable it to accumulate power as well as wealth. But they were reassured by the conviction that prosperity would eventually bring democratisation, and by the knowledge that democracies had seldom gone to war with each other.

Recent findings suggest that for their part, China’s rulers saw the West’s offers of engagement as a trap designed to bring about their own demise. Instead of succumbing to the charms of liberalism, they remained firmly committed to a mercantilist-Leninist governing philosophy, in which the primary purpose of economic activity is not to enhance the welfare of the Chinese people but to bolster the power of the Party and, through it, the nation.

According to recent reports, thus, even as it allowed greater play to market forces, the CCP regime took care to ensure its continued grip at home. And it approached the global economy as another domain of zero-sum struggle, one in which the aim was to strengthen China’s geopolitical position and gain advantage over its rivals.

In a recent development, for a time, the nation’s leaders believed they had little choice but to accept the dangers of increasing interdependence with the West. Once having obtained membership in the WTO, however, Beijing began to take steps to reduce its vulnerability to foreign pressure.

After the turn of the century this derisking strategy advanced along four parallel axes:.

Recent findings suggest that to guard against the possibility of being cut off from vitally needed imports of resources and raw materials, Chinese companies were directed to buy up more overseas mines, oil wells and agricultural land and to build a vast merchant fleet and an elaborate global network of roads, railways and ports to carry their output back home. To reduce exposure to Western tariffs or trade sanctions, Beijing sought upcoming export markets in the global south. To blunt the impact of U.S. financial sanctions, it began to build alternative international payments systems. Finally, to lessen dependence on imported technology China released a series of costly, high-profile technology development programs, began buying cutting-edge Western companies and initiated a campaign of industrial espionage of unprecedented scope and scale.

From the end of the Cold War until the mid-2010s, Washington continued to try to ease Beijing down the path towards economic liberalisation. Together with this persistence, however, there was mounting frustration over China’s trade and industrial policies and its evident failure to live up to the commitments it had made to gain entry to the WTO. As the Chinese economy grew and its level of technological sophistication advanced, these policies appeared to threaten the future prosperity and security of the United States and other industrial democracies.

China’s heavily subsidized exports were hollowing out portions of the American manufacturing base. Relatively easy access to Western companies and universities was helping to speed its technological advance. Its ongoing military buildup and more assertive foreign policy stance darkened perceptions of its intentions and began to make it appear less as a normal trading partner and more like a strategic rival and even a potential foe. Despite all of this, it was not until the very end of Barack Obama’s second term that China’s increasingly forceful efforts to strengthen its position finally began to provoke a meaningful response.

Sources indicate that washington’s belated answer to China’s mercantilist, power-maximising economic policies signalled the start of a two-sided derisking race. The American reaction came first in the form of the experimental and at times spasmodic initiatives of the first Trump administration and then the more coherent, but also limited and cautious approaches pursued by the Biden administration.

Sources indicate that neither Trump nor Biden sought to decouple completely from China, nor did either of them formally abandon the original, ambitious goal of creating an open global economy. Nevertheless, albeit with some hesitation, at least with respect to China the United States started to move away from a predominantly liberal approach to economic relations that emphasized the virtues of openness and the prospect of mutual benefits, towards one that increasingly prioritized power and the pursuit of relative advantage.

America’s derisking campaign comprised several interrelated lines of effort. Regardless of cost, it no longer seemed prudent to depend on a potentially hostile China for minerals, drugs, metals, and chemicals that might be needed in a war or national emergency. To reduce the dangers of dependence, the United States began to use tariffs to constrict imports and subsidies to cultivate alternative sources of supply.

Once seen as a benign byproduct of globalization, the pervasive presence of Chinese-made electronic components and hardware in America’s critical networks now appeared to pose unacceptable risks of espionage or sabotage. Dealing with the problem of penetration by removing these imported products and replacing them with reliable substitutes called for upcoming laws and regulations to guide private companies and government agencies. Finally, slowing the transfer of sensitive technologies required imposing tighter controls on exports and on investment flows both to and from China.

According to recent reports, beijing has reacted to these developments by doubling down. Xi Jinping’s determination to stay the course is due in part to the fact that America’s tougher policies did not come as a surprise. Back in 2002, in the wake of China’s accession to the WTO and the 9/11 attacks, CCP strategists had concluded that they faced a “twenty-year period of strategic opportunity” during which they could grow strong without undue interference from Washington.

Eventually, however, the Americans would turn their attention back to China and, recognizing how much it had grown, they would try even harder to weaken and contain it. At that point Beijing would have no choice but to press ahead.

In the past five years, China has done more to increase security of supplies of food and raw materials, diminish its exposure to financial sanctions, and increase the relative importance of the developing countries as markets for its exports. Together with these defensive measures Beijing has begun to take more aggressive actions. Rather than implement reforms that might have reduced exports and lessened tensions with other nations, it has moved in the opposite direction: ratcheting up subsidies, expanding manufacturing capacity, and boosting exports that threaten to destroy others’ industries and leave them even more reliant on Chinese goods. Chinese firms are also working to dominate global supply chains for critical minerals and other industrial materials. The regime has successfully used the threat of export restrictions on rare earth minerals to pressure America and its democratic partners and is actively seeking to tighten its grip on other potential “chokepoints.”.

The U.S. rejoinder to this intense and purposeful campaign has been mixed and less than fully coherent. Since his return to the White House Donald Trump has expanded on some of the policies that he set in motion during his first term, but he has also taken steps that threaten to undermine their effectiveness.

In a recent development, the second Trump administration has prohibited the importation of Chinese-made drones, robots, and internet routers that could be connected to U.S. telecommunications networks. But it has also ignored the law banning TikTok, a Chinese-controlled social media platform suspected of gathering sensitive information and spreading propaganda, instead negotiating a sale to one of Trump’s domestic political allies.

It has been revealed that to lessen dependence on China, the administration has sought to work with other countries to develop alternative sources of critical minerals. At the same time, in hopes of reviving American industry, it has strained relations with its allies by imposing across-the-board tariffs on their exports, driving countries like Canada closer to Beijing. Finally, since returning to office, Trump has tightened certain restrictions on high tech exports to China while simultaneously loosening export controls on advanced semiconductors crucial to the development of artificial intelligence.

Sources indicate that china’s course in the next stage of the derisking race seems set but America’s remains uncertain. The history of the past century suggests two alternative trajectories. Having failed once again to build a fully integrated global order, the United States may choose not only to distance itself from China but to adopt a posture of omni-directional protectionism and strict “America first” industrial policy as it did after World War I. This risks leaving America isolated as its former friends band together to protect themselves from its own predatory policies as well as China’s.

Recent findings suggest that the aftermath of the Second World War suggests a preferable alternative. Instead of completely abandoning liberal economic principles, Americans could decide instead to narrow the circle in which they are applied to include only those nations that genuinely share and are prepared to defend them. It is only by pooling their resources and better integrating their markets that the advanced democracies can counter a challenge of unprecedented proportions.

It has been revealed that aaron L. Friedberg is a professor emeritus of politics and international affairs at Princeton University. His most recent book is The Derisking Race: China, America, and the Fragmentation of the Global Economy.

#65356. Breaking: The Luxury of Children

Breaking: The Luxury of Children

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JESÚS FERNÁNDEZ-VILLAVERDE is Howard Marks Presidential Professor of Economics at the University of Pennsylvania.
  • Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal.
  • Recent findings suggest that the world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JESÚS FERNÁNDEZ-VILLAVERDE is Howard Marks Presidential Professor of Economics at the University of Pennsylvania. This piece is adapted from “Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World,” co-authored with Patrick Norrick and forthcoming in the 2027 Annual Review of Economics.

Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal.

Recent findings suggest that the world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood. Last year, humanity’s total fertility level dropped below what demographers call the replacement rate—that is, the average number of children that a woman must have to keep a population constant over the long run. This has never happened before. There have been periods when the human population declined because of wars or epidemics, such as the Black Death, in the fourteenth century, or the diseases brought by Europeans to the Americas in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. But now, simply as a function of their choices, humans will see the world population peak around 2055 and then begin to fall.

The story of the coming decades is not simply one of dwindling and aging. There is a great deal of variation in the baby bust. The most surprising trend may be one that has overturned basic assumptions about fertility rates. Where once it was thought that people—and, by extension, countries—with higher levels of income and education would have lower fertility rates than those who were poorer and less educated, the inverse is increasingly true. Many wealthier people and countries boast higher fertility rates than many poor people and countries.

Industry observers note that the inversion is revealing of why governments have had a hard time coming to grips with the fertility crash. The best explanation for why people are no longer having babies is that child-rearing at the scale necessary to maintain populations is fundamentally at odds with the structures of modern life and modern societies. Once an economic necessity, children are now an economic luxury. That portends a world in which economic inequality is accentuated by demographic inequality, with widening fissures within countries and among them. The whole world is grappling with a decline in fertility, but in many different ways. And those differences will stoke further divisions, tensions, and even conflict.

Humanity falling below replacement has passed largely unnoticed. The central projections in the latest release of the United Nations World Population Prospects (in 2024), known as the report’s “medium variant,” still places the world’s total fertility rate slightly above replacement in 2026 and expects the global population to peak as late as 2084. But this medium variant does not fully incorporate the recent drops in births recorded by national statistical agencies, and its projections for future fertility rest on questionable assumptions, including forecasting a strong recovery of fertility rates in countries such as China. By comparison, the report’s “low variant” (the forecast that takes a more pessimistic view of future fertility) accords nearly exactly with my own assessment, which reflects more recent national statistics and takes a less optimistic view on the possible recovery of fertility. In that reading, the world has dropped below replacement fertility levels (approximately 2.2 children per woman) and will only keep dropping.

Fertility rates are plunging so fast that they are overturning many assumptions about demography. The steepest fertility declines have occurred in unexpected countries. Consider this test. Pick the state with the highest fertility rate among the following: Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Jamaica, Iran, Malaysia, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, Sri Lanka, and the United States.

The United States, the wealthiest of the 12, has the highest fertility rate. This holds true even when just assessing the fertility rate of mothers born in the United States (immigrant mothers have a slightly higher fertility rate than native mothers). Dozens of other middle-income countries now have fertility levels below that of the United States.

That trend runs against the old explanation for demographic change, which held that fertility invariably falls as a community or society gets richer. That is demonstrably no longer the case. Among the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), richer members tend to have higher fertility rates than do poorer ones, even after controlling for migration flows. Take Mexico. According to the most recent survey, in 2024, a Mexican woman could expect to have 1.2 children over her lifetime, well below the 1.57 average of non-Hispanic white women in the United States. Mexico’s income per capita is only about 28 percent of the U.S. level. And just two decades ago, fertility rates in Mexico were much higher than those in the United States.

According to recent reports, this dynamic obtains not just among countries but also within them. Richer and more educated households in the United States and other advanced economies now tend to have more children than poorer and less educated ones, reversing a pattern that had held for centuries.

There is no single, simple answer for why this has happened. Most theories do not hold up against international evidence. Factors that seem to contribute to lower fertility in the United States, for instance, such as higher housing prices, don’t seem to matter elsewhere, as many countries have seen even steeper fertility declines without skyrocketing housing prices.

Or take another favorite culprit, smartphones. Some researchers have suggested that the spread of the smartphone stoked atomization and a desire for individual fulfillment, discouraging many people from having children. But fertility rates have been plunging worldwide since the late 1960s, well before smartphones appeared, and there is little evidence of an acceleration in the drop after their introduction. Instead, the device is more likely an accelerator of underlying mechanisms than a cause in itself: by my calculations, smartphones compressed into ten years a change in fertility that would have occurred anyway over 25.

Another common explanation for drops in fertility is the spread of female education and employment. Freed from the domestic function of birthing and raising babies, the argument goes, women have chosen to prioritize other goals instead of child rearing. Although that shift may indeed have played a role in the twentieth century in lowering fertility rates, it is no longer so clearly causal today. Indeed, across OECD countries, the correlation between fertility, on the one hand, and female education and employment, on the other, is positive: the countries where women are more educated and more likely to work outside the home are also the countries with higher fertility rates. And in other regions for which demographers have good vital statistics, such as Latin America, the women not having children in 2026 are the least educated and the ones most likely to not be part of the workforce.

In the absence of neat, definitive explanations, a broader explanation for the global fertility crash comes into view. As societies embrace what is often termed “modernity,” they become incapable of maintaining replacement-level fertility rates. Modernity describes how countries have organized contemporary life around formal institutions (such as schools, universities, and health systems), specialized expertise (through degree accreditation, standardized exams, and professional licensing), and large-scale systems of coordination (such as multinational corporations, governments, and global supply chains). It is not synonymous with capitalism; communist countries, too, invested heavily in mass education and bureaucracies (and saw concomitant declines in fertility). The only way to run large, complex societies that harness modern technology at scale is to standardize knowledge and detach it from local custom through mass education, systems of expertise, and bureaucracies.

In a recent development, modernity raises the cost of children and lowers the cost of childlessness. Parents must equip children with formal knowledge and credentials, an endeavor that takes decades of effort and spending. Tight career schedules also conflict with parents’ biological clocks. The most productive years for a research economist, for example, are usually between 30 and 45. Those are also the years when one needs to spend the most time with children. No matter how much accommodation a university offers, the day still has only 24 hours. Even when a researcher manages to produce both a large family and strong academic output, one can always wonder how much more that researcher would have produced with a smaller family.

And modernity has also made it easier not to have children. In traditional agrarian and artisan economies, children were useful factors of production, helping in the fields and workshops. Children also provided parents and other older relatives with eldercare. But the modern organization of economic life no longer requires children to perform those roles and the advent of welfare states has given the elderly other forms of support. Lineage once determined people’s present and future; it no longer does so in such a comprehensive way.

According to recent reports, there are some exceptions to this seemingly universal trend. Tight-knit religious communities, such as the ultra-Orthodox in Israel and the Amish in the United States, have managed to maintain high fertility rates well above replacement level. But these groups have also stayed apart from much of modern life. For example, the Amish live in rural areas, where housing is much cheaper, and they end formal education at eighth grade, which eliminates one of the main costs of raising a child in a modern society, advanced education.

Apart from these idiosyncratic pockets, modernity has spread around the planet, with fertility falling everywhere. But rates are tumbling unevenly. In 1980, the richer an OECD country, the fewer children its women had. By 2000, the opposite was beginning to become true. The same reversal reveals up inside countries. In Sweden, the demographer Martin Kolk has found that in every cohort born between 1940 and 1970, men with higher lifetime incomes have more children, and that among women born since the 1960s, the poorest have the fewest children. In the United States, the economists Moshe Hazan and Hosny Zoabi have found that in the first decade of the twenty-first century, women with a graduate degree had about 2.0 children, significantly more than the 1.8 for women who stopped at a bachelor’s degree.

Many adults still want to have children and flourishing families. When Gallup asked Americans about their ideal number of children in July 2025, the average answer was 2.7, a figure that has barely changed since the 1970s. But children are costly and bring no income. They have become something of a luxury good that richer people can afford more of than poorer people can. In the same way that a richer household owns, on average, a more expensive car than a poorer one, it also has more children—at least since the 1990s. Prosperous parents can hire help at home, order prepared meals, pay for premium grocery delivery or laundry services, and afford tuition and tutoring.

Recent findings suggest that richer families (and, among them, the most educated parents) also have more stable family lives. For instance, among Americans born between 1957 and 1964 (a cohort whose adult lives can be observed almost in full), about half of men with a high school diploma but no college education had seen their first marriage end in divorce by age 55, compared with 27 percent of men with a bachelor’s degree or more. Stable families lead to higher fertility (and much better outcomes for the children). In short, income and education soften some of the worst consequences of modernity. The intuition of this result applies, as well, to countries as a whole: richer countries can, on average, afford more “luxuries,” including children, than poorer countries.

It has been revealed that if the modernity conjecture is right, the flip in the correlation between income and fertility that is evident within OECD countries will extend to all other countries over the next few decades. This is already happening in the Americas: among countries with at least 20 million inhabitants, the United States has the highest fertility rate in the hemisphere, well ahead of Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, and Mexico, and matched only by Peru, whose fertility rate is plummeting fast. (Venezuela’s official fertility rate is pure fiction.).

It has been revealed that the same phenomenon will occur in sub-Saharan Africa over the next few decades. It is often projected that the continent’s high fertility rates will make up for shortfalls elsewhere—but that will likely not happen. Indeed, in those sub-Saharan African countries for which demographers have slightly better statistical data, fertility rates are dropping very rapidly. For example, a recent household survey in the Republic of Congo has shown a decrease in fertility from 5.1 children per woman in 2011–12 to 3.5 in 2025. Similar falls are happening elsewhere and likely to accelerate as sub-Saharan Africa succumbs to the same factors that have sped fertility declines elsewhere.

The coming years will produce deep changes in populations within countries and across countries. The already sharp divide between regions and social groups with higher average incomes and education levels and those with lower average incomes and education levels will grow more pronounced, with the added dimension of contrasting fertility rates. The school district of a wealthy suburb outside a major East Coast city may not need to grapple with the widespread school closings that urban districts are already experiencing. And since political power in a democracy follows, at least to some extent, the number of voters, these different regions and social groups will see their relative influence in American politics change: New York, for instance, has lost 19 votes in the electoral college since the 1940s.

Something similar can happen among countries. In 1972, nearly eight times as many children were born in China as in the United States. In 2025, that figure has dropped to 2.2 times as many. China’s total fertility rate in 2025 was 0.93, while the U.S. rate was 1.58. If fertility rates remain at those levels, the United States will overtake China in annual births at some point in the 2080s and in total population by around 2120. That date might arrive earlier if the gap between the fertility rates of China and the United States continues to widen.

Demography is not necessarily destiny, but a world in which the United States has a larger population than China is very different from the world today. The shrinking and aging of populations will have first-order effects on a country’s economic performance. In research with Gustavo Ventura and Wen Yao, I have documented that nearly all of Japan’s poor economic performance relative to the United States since 1990 can be explained by its worse demographics, not by financial crises or poor economic policy. Among the great powers, the United States is the least exposed to demographic headwinds. Younger populations tend to be more innovative and less reliant on public support, a fact that bodes well for American prospects in the competition to come.

But for most other countries, demographic decline will produce significant problems. Aging Japan, for instance, is likely the best-case scenario for countries reaching a demographic sunset. It boasts a capable state and a homogeneous society with a high degree of consensus. More important, Japan became rich before it got old. Countries such as Mexico and Thailand, which lack many of Japan’s advantages, may struggle to weather the same demographic headwinds. While rich economies can rely on immigration to soften some of the effects of falling fertility, countries such as Tunisia or Bolivia, which lose many people to emigration, may find it harder to deal with their own baby busts. The latest dynamics of fertility augur a world in which gaps between the haves and the have-nots grow even wider, as poorer countries and communities endure strains that wealthier countries and communities manage to escape.

According to recent reports, short of an unlikely turn to the social mores of deeply conservative and ideological communities, such as the Amish, only transformations in material circumstances will help raise fertility rates. Governments have had a hard time determining how to tackle fertility decline. Policy can do only so much in convincing people to make the monumental decision to have children. But that does not mean that governments should not try to reverse these trends. Their policies should respect the freedom of citizens to form the families they believe are best for them. Ultralow fertility seems to be caused not by a lack of desire for children but by the absence of the conditions that would make having children easier, or even possible.

Industry observers note that in this vein, some policies are no-brainers. Governments should make education systems more accessible and less competitive than, for example, the ones found in East Asia and in the United States, where high levels of cost and stress discourage having children. They should build more affordable housing and provide more affordable childcare. Such material changes may have only a marginal impact on rates, but even, for instance, raising the U.S. total fertility rate to 1.7 from the current 1.58 would produce a significant impact. Fertility rates behave like the rates of return on a retirement fund: small yearly differences accumulate into large differences over time. Policies that give people greater material freedom to have children can thus be very consequential in the long term.

If governments fail to enact these policies, and if, indeed, these policies fail to encourage a broader rise in fertility, the world will simply become more unequal. Richer families and richer countries will gain greater weight in the population, while poorer families and poorer countries dwindle and weaken. These shifts will create political tensions, as shrinking populations will add to their relative poverty the desperate sense that they have no demographic future. Eastern Germany offers a preview. Since reunification, its young people (above all, its young women) have left for western Germany, its towns have emptied and aged, and its voters have turned to the parties at both extremes of the political spectrum. Many countries in the world are about to become eastern Germany, but few of them will have a western Germany to pay the bills. Demographers often suggest that the world is united by the crash in fertility rates. In truth, demographic decline will likely divide the world even further.

Breaking: The U.S. Tech Outage Wave, Explained

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

In a recent development, A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

Sources indicate that A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

Given the outages occurred on such a massive scale and in quick succession, questions have been raised as to whether they were a result of nefarious activities. But there is at the moment no evidence that the recent incidents were due to cyberattacks or that they were linked.

The Microsoft outage was the result of a combination of factors, including a “latent bug” from July that caused servers to become “overwhelmed and unresponsive,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, agents, and platform, stated in a post on X. Lamanna said a “surge in load” and decreased server capacity had also contributed to the outage.

Recent findings suggest that the FAA is still assessing what led to the ground stop, which lasted less than five hours, but a preliminary investigation indicated that the technical problem was caused by the installation of a router at a radio facility in Arkansas that may have flooded its communications network. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, is also being looked at as part of the inquiry.

The short-lived Chase Bank outage on Monday, which led to complications with processing transactions and seemingly had a ripple effect that caused problems for customers at other banks, was the result of a “software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” the bank mentioned in a post on X, adding that “there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” Apple said the outage it experienced on Tuesday, which lasted hours and disrupted the Apple Store and other services, was the result of an “internal update” and not due to a cyberattack.

Industry observers note that the NSA disruption, which reportedly caused the agency’s internal communications network for highly classified information, NSANet, to go offline, had a similarly prosaic cause. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency stated in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”.

The Trump administration has acknowledged the unease the outages have caused among the public while emphasizing that there are right now no indications that any were tied to a cyberattack or coordinated by outside actors.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”.

Sources indicate that secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday recognized that people are “fearful” and “uncertain,” but he was unequivocal: “We are not under systemic attack,” he mentioned. “These events—one has nothing to do with the other. They are not interrelated.”.

According to recent reports, but it makes sense that people are on edge about technology and how its dominance over modern life can make societies vulnerable. All of these incidents came on the heels of a series of suspected cyberattacks on supermarket freezers in Europe that caused millions of dollars in damage. They’ve also come at a time when anxiety over the rapid development of artificial intelligence has reached a fever pitch.

It doesn’t help that these outages hit as the increasingly symbiotic relationship between AI and the stock market was on many people’s minds amid the chaos swirling around Nvidia—following a salacious scandal that led to the resignation of the tech giant’s co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang.

And national security and tech experts say AI may be partly to blame for these disruptions—though not in the way you might think. AI tools are increasingly helping organizations to identify vulnerabilities in their computer systems. That’s mostly a good thing because those flaws can then be fixed before any potential bad actors can exploit them. But those fixes don’t always go smoothly.

“AI code scanning has caused a tidal wave of vulnerability discovery,” and companies and government agencies are “rushing to make updates and fix” those vulnerabilities, David Agranovich, a director for intelligence on the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, remarked in a post on X. “[E]specially with legacy infrastructure, it can be incredibly hard to predict all of the different dependencies that might break because of those patches. The pace of manual patching has a cost, and that cost is reliability,” Agranovich added. “The result is many cascading and disparate system outages.”.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a co-chair of the Senate Cybersecurity Caucus, offered a similar assessment. Warner said in a statement on Tuesday that he understood why Americans were so concerned about the widespread outages and underscored that there is “no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort.” But he added that what appears to be happening is a “consequence of how promptly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape.”.

AI has opened the door to “identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner mentioned.

The recent disruptions should serve as a “wake-up call” on the ways in which AI is “moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner mentioned, reiterating his call for “commonsense guardrails on AI and stronger cybersecurity protections.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SOLRITE and sonnen plan to digitally integrate VPP smart breakers into what the companies are calling the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The expanded VPP Node combines sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to manage major household loads. The VPP smart breaker, controlled by ADAPT Energy, can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be used for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” noted Regan George, CEO and founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”.

Recent findings suggest that the system can shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns.

This integration is designed to manage whole-home electrical loads in the background, not requiring homeowners to reset circuits during an outage.

In a recent development, “This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”.

When a VPP event happens, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid.

In a recent development, “With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” remarked Blake Richetta, chairman and CEO of sonnen. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”.

#65351. China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2492 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
  • Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI?
  • Beijing has long appreciated this dynamic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. He served as AI Policy Coordinator in the Office of the Special Envoy for Critical and Emerging Technology at the State Department from 2023 to 2025.

And America Should Be Taking Notes.

Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI? That is the question driving debates in Washington about the wisdom of pursuing talks on the subject with Beijing. The Biden administration paired sweeping technology restrictions with a narrow dialogue on risk, and the Trump administration has kept a channel open even as it has downplayed safety. Some experts go further. They hope that cooperation on safety can be siloed off from competition entirely, a belief as appealing as it is fanciful. Any dialogue on AI risk takes place within the broader strategic competition between the United States and China.

Beijing has long appreciated this dynamic. Much of Washington has not. Whereas the United States has shifted its approach to AI competition and safety across and within presidential administrations, Beijing has kept its AI diplomacy focused on gaining competitive advantage over the United States. China has taken part in international AI safety discussions, but it has used them, along with talks with the United States, to paint U.S. export controls as the main obstacle to cooperation. It has cast itself as the champion of the developing world, promising a Chinese-led AI ecosystem without technological or financial barriers as an alternative to a restrictive U.S.-led AI order. The pitch is working. A growing number of states are embracing China’s message, and Chinese open-weight models are gaining users across the developing world.

It has been revealed that if the United States wants to maintain its lead and make meaningful progress on safety, it needs to treat the dialogue as part of the competition with China. To do so, it must ramp up pressure on China outside the talks and offer countries still choosing sides a more compelling vision for AI adoption and governance. And when U.S. and Chinese officials next meet, in November, Washington should test Beijing’s seriousness about safety. In short, the United States should approach AI diplomacy with the same strategic clarity China has.

The Biden administration’s first round of advanced semiconductor export controls in October 2022 and the release of ChatGPT a month later signaled that the United States had taken an early lead in the AI competition and would act to weaken China’s AI industry. Washington and its allies also seized the diplomatic initiative, taking the first steps toward global AI governance. In May 2023, the G-7 began intense discussions on AI governance that would eventually produce a code of conduct for developers. Weeks later, the United Kingdom announced it would host the first global AI safety summit at Bletchley Park.

According to recent reports, china responded by rolling out a diplomatic script it has been honing ever since. Its core tenets first appeared in the Global AI Governance Initiative, published in October 2023. It called for countries to “put equal emphasis on development and security” (though it left security to be defined by individual states) and contrasted China’s focus on cooperation and development with U.S. export controls, attacking Washington for “creating barriers and disrupting the global AI supply chain through technological monopolies and unilateral coercive measures.” Despite Beijing’s growing body of AI regulations at home, the initiative offered little more than slogans on the technology’s risks.

Recent findings suggest that that basic formula—cooperation and development, set against U.S. restrictions, with little to say about risk—has guided China’s AI diplomacy for the last three years. In March 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a U.S.-led resolution on safe, secure, and trustworthy AI intended to appeal to both developed and developing countries. China supported the resolution, then introduced another resolution centered on help for poorer countries and “emphasizing that member states should enjoy equal opportunities” to develop and use AI. At a UN Security Council meeting on AI chaired by the United States in December that year, China’s UN ambassador, Fu Cong, once again counterposed Beijing’s stated interest in cooperation against “discriminatory barriers based on ideological differences.” In thinly veiled terms, Fu was charging that U.S. restrictions on China harmed the developing world.

It has been revealed that to win the support of these countries as they built out their AI infrastructure, China needed a bloc of its own. In July 2025, Premier Li Qiang proposed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which promised developing countries technology, training, and a greater say in writing global AI rules. In a speech marking its launch a year later, Chinese leader Xi Jinping called for “openness,” shorthand for access to U.S. chips and the adoption of Chinese open-weight models. After urging countries to take the risks of AI seriously, Xi added that they should, “in the meantime,” jointly oppose “overstretching the national security concept in the field of AI and placing one country’s security over that of others.” Cooperation on risks, in Xi’s telling, was subordinate to overcoming U.S. restrictions.

In a recent development, WAICO has promptly gained standing among its target audience. An early endorsement by UN Secretary-General António Guterres lent it immediate credibility in the eyes of developing countries, and Chinese officials have since promoted WAICO in frequent speeches and in bilateral meetings with countries as varied as Brazil, Pakistan, and Serbia. Beijing has signaled that membership will come with perks. Its draft export controls on leading models, released in October, promise to help WAICO’s 37 members build their AI capabilities, suggesting members could have easier access to models restricted for the rest of the world.

Industry observers note that xi personally led this diplomatic offensive in the lead-up to the Washington summit with U.S. President Donald Trump in September. During a speech in Kyrgyzstan, he pledged to expand a Chinese AI center for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization that helps members build local language models and train engineers. In Cairo, he and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi signed agreements on AI, data centers, and semiconductors, which have become a staple of Xi’s trips abroad. And in Newly introduced Delhi, Xi proposed an open-source AI zone for BRICS members and told other leaders that a “small yard, high fences” approach would only “box oneself in and divide the world.” AI risks were nowhere on the agenda. The message instead was that U.S. restrictions would isolate Washington, not Beijing.

Sources indicate that much of the allure of China’s pitch rests on how the country’s developers share their technology. Chinese developers release their best models with open weights, which any government or company can download, run on its own hardware, and adapt to its own language. For governments wary of depending on American companies whose exports Washington can restrict, open-weight models promise a greater degree of control. Chinese developers rarely conduct or publish the results of any safety testing for these models, leaving others to discover after release whether, for example, they can be used to launch cyberattacks or build weapons. But their accessibility allows Beijing to argue that any effort to contain the risks of Chinese models is an attempt to deny AI to the developing world.

In a recent development, china’s approach to bilateral AI talks with the United States has deflected discussions of risk just as assiduously as its global AI diplomacy has. In May 2024, the United States and China held talks in Geneva, which I joined as part of the U.S. delegation. The U.S. objective of the talks was to test whether an in-depth technical exchange with China on AI risk was possible. The answer was no. Chinese diplomats steered the discussion away from risks for hours and declined to even explain China’s own AI regulations beyond a superficial overview, despite having technical experts from the relevant agencies in the room.

It has been revealed that the Chinese position came through most clearly in the opening and closing remarks of the delegation’s most senior officials. They began with an appeal for cooperation on capacity-building projects in the developing world. They then cast U.S. technology restrictions as an attempt to contain China’s development and the U.S. emphasis on safety as a barrier preventing developing countries from accessing and using AI. The implication was clear—export controls were the primary impediment to cooperation on AI safety. The one concrete outcome, a November 2024 statement in which former President Joe Biden and Xi affirmed “the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons,” asked little of Beijing.

Sources indicate that this September, after the summit between Trump and Xi in Washington, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs published an “eight-point consensus,” Beijing’s account of what the two sides had agreed to. It described the dialogue as an exchange on the “risks and benefits” of AI. But whereas the White House framed the dialogue as a security concern, listing it alongside nuclear arms control, China’s Ministry of Commerce stressed instead that talks had taken place, and would continue, under the two countries’ economic and trade mechanism. Folded into trade talks, a dialogue on AI risks and benefits leaves Beijing free to parry U.S. requests on risks, such as limits on openly releasing models with dangerous capabilities, by demanding that Washington relax export controls.

According to recent reports, xi did propose to “jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” conveniently eliding China’s own frequent use of AI against the United States in various ways, such as hacking campaigns and influence operations. He added that AI should remain under human control and be developed for good, a principle Beijing has repeated since 2023 but about which it has offered little further detail or follow-through. More pointed was his insistence that future dialogue should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other” and his request that Chinese companies be “treated fairly,” both implicit rebukes of U.S. restrictions.

This record suggests Beijing will come to future meetings, beginning with the next discussion in November, with proposals designed to put Washington in a bind. Although U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has made clear that export controls are not on the table, Beijing will raise them anyway. If Washington engages, Chinese negotiators will claim a standing channel where U.S. restrictions on AI technology are up for negotiation. If it refuses, Beijing will continue to evade U.S. entreaties on safety while accusing Washington of stifling opportunity for developing countries. It hopes that every round of the dialogue will further cement an impression among allies such as Japan and the Netherlands that Washington will trade away restrictions over their heads, and that they should accommodate China’s AI ambitions, too.

But Washington is in a stronger position than its diplomacy has let on. The world’s leading models are still American, and, together with allies, the United States controls key chokepoints in the semiconductor supply chain. Export controls on those chokepoints are not a bargaining chip and should be strengthened. Chinese AI companies regularly lament their lack of high-end chips and have resorted to smuggling chips and illicitly distilling U.S. models. U.S. developers also conduct increasingly extensive and transparent safety testing, which Chinese developers avoid. Taken together, these strengths give Washington the means to press Beijing and an attractive offer for the rest of the world. It should use them, advertising its rigorously tested models to compete for global adoption while pressuring China on safety in the dialogue.

In a recent development, the first chance to apply that pressure is the next bilateral meeting. Washington should set two conditions for it and future meetings. Chinese developers must commit to publishing safety evaluations at least as extensive as those that leading U.S. developers publish today on equivalent benchmarks for the most serious risks, such as cyberattacks and biological weapons, and to disclosing previous and future incidents. The United States can make the same commitments, as its companies already publish such evaluations, increasingly disclose incidents, and open their models to independent and government evaluators before release. Otherwise, the incident channel to which the two sides agreed in September will run one way, with China free to point to U.S. incidents while reporting none of its own.

These conditions would change the terms of the dialogue. Since 2023, Washington has raised risks and Beijing has steered the conversation toward development. As long as Chinese companies face no scrutiny for the risks of their models, Beijing can tout them for their openness and innovation without having to answer questions from the rest of the world about their safety. Concordia AI, which tracks China’s AI ecosystem, found that only five of China’s ten leading developers published safety test results for any model over the past year, and none did so consistently. If China agrees, governments and companies choosing which models to use will be able to judge Chinese and American developers by the same criteria. If China refuses, the onus will be on Beijing to explain why fair treatment for Chinese companies should not extend to safety testing. Regardless, the U.S. government should ramp up its own tests of new Chinese models and publish the results. It should also avoid unforced errors, such as Trump’s waving away of AI safety concerns as a “hoax,” which hand Beijing an easy retort to U.S. appeals.

In a recent development, more broadly, effective AI diplomacy ultimately requires convincing other countries to join the American AI ecosystem. Countries that train their engineers, build their local language models, and run their data centers on Chinese technology will come to depend on it. To counter that dependence (and prevent it from turning into political alignment), Washington needs to present a positive vision of AI governance that pairs verifiable safety commitments—the kind Chinese developers avoid—with the access and investment developing countries want.

According to recent reports, U.S. companies already offer the best technology, but Washington has yet to put real diplomatic weight behind them. It should draw from its evolving approach at home to rally partners around shared safety measures. Under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed in September, six leading U.S. companies committed themselves to internal controls, external audits, and independent oversight. The G-7 Code of Conduct, which built on voluntary commitments secured under the Biden administration, could incorporate the accord’s measures and serve as a common standard for partners. Countries that agree to its measures could receive priority for technology and financing. Without such incentives, the AI competition may be determined by price and access alone, where China has the edge.

According to recent reports, much of Washington has treated talks with Beijing as a place to manage the shared risks of AI apart from the competition. China has always treated them as an arena of the larger rivalry. To maintain its lead and make real progress on safety, the United States should start doing the same.
